response.answer: Prof. Deepak Kumar Jha is a leading researcher in Pleistocene population dynamics and early human dispersals in western Europe. He has published extensively on Quaternary environments and human-environment interactions. His work includes agent-based modeling of hominin dispersals.

results.title: Hominid dispersals in Europe - Wikipedia
results.content: **Hominid dispersals in Europe** refers to the colonisation "Colonisation (biology)") of the European continent by various species of hominid, including hominins and archaic and modern humans. Prior to arriving in Europe, the source of hominids appeared to be East Africa, where stone tools and hominid fossils are the most abundant and recorded. Short and repetitive migrations of archaic humans before 1 million years ago suggest that their residence in Europe was not permanent at the time. Besides the findings from East Anglia, the first constant presence of archaic humans in Europe begins 500,000–600,000 years ago. Arising in Europe at least 400,000 years ago, the Neanderthal archaic humans (a descendant of *Homo heidelbergensis*) would become more stable residents of the continent. Neanderthals were present both in the Middle East and in Europe, and the arriving populations of anatomically modern humans (also known as "Cro-Magnon" or European early modern humans) have interbred with Neanderthal populations to a limited degree.

results.title: The Middle Pleistocene population of Europe could have reached 25,000
results.content: # The Middle Pleistocene population of Europe could have reached 25,000. **The Middle Pleistocene population of Europe could have reached 25,000 individuals**. Ana Mateos and Jesús Rodríguez, scientists at the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana (CENIEH), have led the international team that has published a paper in the journal *Scientific Reports*, showing that the human population of western Europe could have been larger and more widely distributed than was believed, and perhaps reached 25,000 individuals. This work was performed in collaboration with the geographers Christian Willmes, of the University of Cologne, and Christian Sommer, of the University of Tübingen, as part of the project TROPHIc. The period from 350,000 to 550,000 to years ago was crucial for human evolution in Europe, as this was when the process that would give rise to the Neanderthals started and the foundations were laid for the development of Levallois, a new stone tool manufacturing technology.
